gloss: To take part in a contest and try to do better than the others.
examples: Only eight teams *compete* in the final round.
She *competed* in three events last summer.
He has been *competing* at this level since he was nine.
contrast: Takes prepositions, never a direct object: *compete **against** a rival*, *compete **for** a medal*, *compete **in** an event*.

transitivity: both — transitive (that win qualifies them), intransitive (qualify for the final)
gloss: To reach the standard needed to enter the next stage of a competition.
examples: The top four *qualify* for the semifinals.
He *qualified* for the Olympics by a tenth of a second.
Our team has *qualified* three years in a row.
contrast: The *-y* becomes *-ies* and *-ied*: *qualifies*, *qualified*, but *qualifying* keeps the y. Qualify **for** something.

gloss: To take part in an activity or event together with other people.
examples: All sixth graders *participate* in the field day.
She *participated* in the relay and the long jump.
More than three hundred runners are *participating* this year.
contrast: Always participate **in** something, never *participate to*.

gloss: To compete seriously for something such as a title or a prize.
examples: Three clubs *contend* for the title almost every season.
They *contended* for the championship until the final week.
He has been *contending* with a knee injury all year.
contrast: Contend **for** a prize; contend **with** a problem or a rival.

transitivity: both — transitive (dominate the league), intransitive (she dominated from the start)
gloss: To be much stronger than everyone else in a game or a sport.
examples: Tall centers *dominate* under the basket.
Brazil *dominated* the second half.
She has *dominated* the sport for almost a decade.

gloss: To play much better than an opponent during a game.
examples: On a good day they can *outplay* anyone in the state.
The visitors *outplayed* us in every position.
We were *outplayed* from the opening whistle.

ru: набирать больше очков, обыгрывать по очкам
gloss: To score more points or goals than the other side.
examples: They *outscore* their opponents by twenty points a game.
Miami *outscored* Boston 30-12 in the fourth quarter.
Our front line has *outscored* every other team in the league.

gloss: To keep going longer than someone else and so win.
examples: In this heat the fitter team will simply *outlast* the other.
She *outlasted* four opponents to reach the final.
He has *outlasted* three head coaches at the same club.

gloss: To be so much better than an opponent that the contest is never close.
examples: A veteran can *outclass* a rookie without even running hard.
The champions *outclassed* us in every department.
Our juniors were badly *outclassed* by the visiting school.

gloss: To move faster than someone and leave them behind.
examples: Very few defenders can *outpace* him over ten yards.
She *outpaced* the whole field on the last lap.
He has *outpaced* every sprinter he has met this season.

gloss: To go beyond a previous record, result, or level.
examples: Few players *surpass* him for stamina.
She *surpassed* the old record by two full seconds.
Attendance has already *surpassed* last year's total.
contrast: A verb ending in *-ss* adds *-es* in the third person: *surpasses*, not *surpasss*.

gloss: To knock a team or player out of a competition so that they cannot continue.
examples: One more loss will *eliminate* them from the playoffs.
A late goal *eliminated* the defending champions.
Two seeded players have already been *eliminated*.

gloss: To win something definitely, so that no later result can change it.
examples: A win tonight would *clinch* the division.
They *clinched* a playoff spot with two games to spare.
The title was *clinched* back in October.

gloss: To keep a title or trophy that you already hold.
examples: The champion hopes to *retain* the belt in May.
She *retained* her title for a fourth straight year.
He has *retained* the trophy since 2019.

gloss: To beat a champion and take their title away.
examples: Nobody expected a rookie to *dethrone* the champion.
They *dethroned* the winners of the last two seasons.
The long-time favorite was finally *dethroned* in Paris.

gloss: To officially name someone the winner or champion.
examples: The league will *crown* a new champion tonight.
They *crowned* him rookie of the year.
She was *crowned* world champion in Oslo.

gloss: To finish high enough in a competition to win a medal.
examples: Only three swimmers *medal* in each event.
He *medaled* in the two hundred meters.
She has *medaled* at two straight world championships.
contrast: American English keeps one l: *medaled*, *medaling*. British writing doubles it: *medalled*.

gloss: To score a goal that makes the score level again.
examples: They need one more goal to *equalize*.
The striker *equalized* in the eighty-eighth minute.
United had already *equalized* twice before halftime.
contrast: American spelling uses *-ize*; British writing often prefers *equalise*.

gloss: To beat an opponent by a very large margin.
examples: On their home field they *trounce* almost everybody.
We *trounced* the visitors six to nothing.
They have been *trounced* in both road games.

gloss: To defeat a team completely and heavily.
examples: A healthy squad can *rout* this team.
The Tigers *routed* their rivals by forty points.
Our defense was *routed* in the second half.
contrast: *Rout* rhymes with *out*. Do not confuse it with the noun *route* (a way to go), which Americans say /ruːt/ or /raʊt/.

gloss: To score a number of points, or to add up the scores.
examples: The judges *tally* the scores after every round.
She *tallied* eighteen points in the first half.
The votes for most valuable player are being *tallied* now.
contrast: Consonant + *-y* becomes *-ies* and *-ied*: *tallies*, *tallied*, but *tallying* keeps the y.

gloss: To win or record a result and add it to your total.
examples: They can *notch* their tenth win tonight.
He *notched* three assists in the opener.
She has *notched* five victories in a row.

transitivity: both — transitive (net a goal), intransitive (he netted again on Sunday)
gloss: To put the ball into the goal and score.
examples: A striker like that can *net* twenty goals a season.
She *netted* the winner in extra time.
He has *netted* in four straight games.
contrast: One short vowel before a final t, so the t doubles: *netted*, *netting*.

gloss: To match a record or a result that someone else has already set.
examples: A time of 9.8 would *equal* the school record.
She *equaled* the world record in Rome.
That mark has never been *equaled* since.
contrast: American English keeps one l: *equaled*, *equaling*. British writing doubles it: *equalled*.

ru: обгонять на круг, обойти на круг
gloss: To get a whole lap ahead of a slower competitor in a race.
examples: The leaders *lap* the slowest riders twice.
He *lapped* half the field by mile ten.
Two cars had been *lapped* before the first pit stop.
contrast: One short vowel before a final p, so the p doubles: *lapped*, *lapping*.

gloss: To win, especially after a hard struggle.
examples: Underdogs rarely *triumph* on this court.
Spain *triumphed* on penalties.
She has *triumphed* over three former champions.
contrast: Triumph **over** an opponent. The *ph* is said /f/: TRY-uhmf.

gloss: To win in the end, especially in a close contest.
examples: Talent does not always *prevail* over hard work.
Our team *prevailed* in a third-set tiebreak.
The home side has *prevailed* in nine straight meetings.
contrast: Prevail **over** or **against** an opponent.

transitivity: both — transitive (coach a team), intransitive (he coaches at the high school)
gloss: To train a player or a team and direct how they play.
examples: He wants to *coach* high school football.
She *coached* the team to two state titles.
He has been *coaching* here for twenty years.

gloss: To guide and advise a less experienced player over a long period.
examples: The veterans *mentor* the younger players.
She *mentored* three future champions.
He has been *mentoring* the young goalkeeper all season.

gloss: To lead a team as its captain.
examples: She will *captain* the national team this summer.
He *captained* the squad for six seasons.
The side has been *captained* by the same player since 2020.

transitivity: both — transitive (scout a player), intransitive (he scouts for a college team)
gloss: To watch players or opposing teams in order to judge them.
examples: Clubs *scout* players as young as fourteen.
They *scouted* him at a high school tournament.
Our staff has been *scouting* the opposition all week.

ru: сажать на скамейку запасных, оставить в запасе
gloss: To take a player out of the game and keep them on the bench.
examples: The coach may *bench* him for the final.
They *benched* their starting goalkeeper.
He was *benched* after two poor games.

transitivity: both — transitive (substitute a tired player), intransitive (he substituted for the injured captain)
gloss: To put one player onto the field in place of another.
examples: Coaches may *substitute* five players per game.
She was *substituted* at halftime.
They are *substituting* the tired forwards now.
contrast: You substitute a fresh player **for** a tired one, or substitute the tired one **with** a fresh one. Both patterns are used; keep them straight.

transitivity: both — transitive (rest a player), intransitive (rest between sets)
gloss: To stop training or playing for a while so the body recovers.
examples: Runners *rest* two minutes between intervals.
The manager *rested* his best players before the cup game.
She has been *resting* a sore shoulder for a week.

gloss: To gather in a tight circle to plan the next play.
examples: The players *huddle* before every snap.
The whole team *huddled* around the coach.
They were still *huddling* when the whistle blew.

gloss: To play a practice game that does not count in the standings.
examples: The two squads *scrimmage* every Thursday.
We *scrimmaged* against the junior team.
They have been *scrimmaging* in full pads all week.
contrast: Double m in the middle: *scrimmage*, not *scrimage*.

gloss: To stop competing for good at the end of a career.
examples: Most gymnasts *retire* before they turn twenty-five.
He *retired* after the 2022 season.
She has *retired* from international play but still coaches.
contrast: Retire **from** a sport. The ending keeps its schwa: /rɪˈtaɪər/, ri-TY-ur, not ri-TYR.

ru: выводить из строя (о травме), лишать игровой практики
gloss: To keep a player out of the game, usually because of injury.
examples: A hamstring strain can *sideline* a sprinter for weeks.
The injury *sidelined* him for two months.
Their captain has been *sidelined* since March.
contrast: Most often used in the passive: *he was sidelined by a knee injury*.

gloss: To train the body so that it is fit and strong for a sport.
examples: Coaches *condition* the squad for six weeks before the season.
He *conditioned* himself with long runs in the hills.
The team has been *conditioning* since June.

gloss: To play with constant energy and effort, chasing every ball.
examples: Good players *hustle* on every single play.
She *hustled* back on defense after the turnover.
He has been *hustling* for loose balls all night.
contrast: The t is silent: HUS-uhl, like *whistle* and *castle*.

ru: переводить в низший дивизион, понижать в классе
gloss: To move a team down into a lower division at the end of a season.
examples: Two more defeats would *relegate* the club.
They *relegated* three teams that year instead of two.
The club was *relegated* last spring for the first time.
contrast: Usually passive from the team's point of view: *they were relegated*, not *they relegated*.

transitivity: both — transitive (referee a game), intransitive (he referees on weekends)
gloss: To control a game and make sure the rules are followed.
examples: Retired players often *referee* youth games.
He *refereed* two World Cup finals.
She has been *refereeing* for fifteen years.
contrast: The double e stays in every form: *refereed*, *refereeing* — three e's in a row.

transitivity: both — transitive (umpire a match), intransitive (he umpires in the summer league)
gloss: To act as the official who judges play in baseball, tennis, or cricket.
examples: Volunteers *umpire* the Little League games.
He *umpired* behind the plate for all nine innings.
She has *umpired* at three US Opens.

transitivity: both — transitive (officiate a bout), intransitive (he officiates at college level)
gloss: To serve as a referee, umpire, or judge at a sporting event.
examples: Two judges *officiate* each bout.
He *officiated* the championship game.
She has been *officiating* college basketball since 2015.

transitivity: both — transitive (foul the shooter), intransitive (he fouled twice in a minute)
gloss: To break the rules by hitting, holding, or tripping an opponent.
examples: Defenders *foul* him every time he drives to the basket.
She *fouled* the shooter with a second left.
He had already been *fouled* twice in the opening minute.

gloss: To give a player an official warning for breaking the rules.
examples: Referees *caution* players for wasting time.
The referee *cautioned* both captains.
He had been *cautioned* earlier in the half.

gloss: To cancel another official's decision by using greater authority.
examples: Video review can *overrule* the referee on the field.
The chair umpire *overruled* the line call.
His decision was *overruled* after a replay.
contrast: Two r's meet in the middle: *over* + *rule* = *overrule*.

transitivity: both — transitive (appeal the ruling), intransitive (appeal to the federation)
gloss: To formally ask for a decision or a punishment to be changed.
examples: The team will *appeal* the suspension.
She *appealed* to the tournament committee the same evening.
The red card has already been *appealed*.
contrast: Appeal **to** a person or body, appeal **against** a decision. American writing also allows the direct object: *appeal the ban*.

gloss: To measure how long someone takes to do something.
examples: The coaches *time* every sprint.
They *timed* her at 11.4 seconds.
All the laps are being *timed* electronically.
contrast: The silent e drops before *-ing*: *timing*, never *timeing*.

gloss: To record a particular time or speed for someone.
examples: Scouts want to see him *clock* under 4.5 seconds.
She *clocked* a personal best in the heats.
The pitcher was *clocked* at ninety-nine miles an hour.

transitivity: both — transitive (dribble the ball), intransitive (dribble up the court)
gloss: To move the ball along with small touches or bounces while running.
examples: Young players learn to *dribble* with both hands.
He *dribbled* past three defenders.
She was *dribbling* up the sideline when the whistle blew.

ru: отбирать мяч; блокировать, сбивать с ног
gloss: To bring down an opponent or take the ball away from them.
examples: Linebackers *tackle* the runner behind the line.
He *tackled* the striker just outside the box.
The quarterback was *tackled* for a nine-yard loss.

gloss: To catch or stop a pass that was meant for someone else.
examples: Good defenders *intercept* lazy passes.
She *intercepted* the ball at midfield and ran.
Two of his throws were *intercepted* in the first quarter.

ru: бить с лёта, играть с лёта
transitivity: both — transitive (volley the cross), intransitive (she volleys well at the net)
gloss: To hit a ball before it bounces.
examples: She likes to *volley* at the net.
He *volleyed* the cross into the top corner.
The ball was *volleyed* home from six yards out.
contrast: Vowel + y, so the y stays: *volleys*, *volleyed* — not *vollies* or *vollied*.

gloss: To hit the ball hard and downward over the net.
examples: Their tall hitters *spike* from the back row.
She *spiked* the ball straight down the line.
He was *spiking* well all match.

gloss: To hit or throw the ball in a high slow curve over someone.
examples: Try to *lob* the ball over the goalkeeper.
She *lobbed* the return over his head.
He has been *lobbing* every short ball all afternoon.
contrast: One short vowel before a final b, so the b doubles: *lobbed*, *lobbing*.

ru: бить патт, катить мяч в лунку (гольф)
transitivity: both — transitive (putt the ball), intransitive (he putts beautifully)
gloss: To hit a golf ball gently along the green toward the hole.
examples: He can *putt* better than anyone on tour.
She *putted* from thirty feet and made it.
He was *putting* for birdie on the last hole.
contrast: *Putt* rhymes with *cut* /pʌt/; the everyday verb *put* is /pʊt/. Both, confusingly, give *putting*.

ru: выбивать мяч с рук, делать пант
transitivity: both — transitive (punt the ball away), intransitive (on fourth down they punt)
gloss: To kick the ball after dropping it from your hands, giving it to the other team.
examples: On fourth down they usually *punt*.
He *punted* from his own end zone.
The ball was *punted* fifty-two yards.

transitivity: both — transitive (bat the ball into left field), intransitive (she bats third)
gloss: To take your turn hitting the ball with a bat.
examples: Left-handers usually *bat* against right-handed pitching.
He *batted* .310 last season.
She has been *batting* leadoff all year.
contrast: One short vowel before a final t, so the t doubles: *batted*, *batting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (bunt the runner over), intransitive (he bunted to move the runner)
gloss: In baseball, to tap the ball softly instead of swinging at it.
examples: With a runner on first, you *bunt*.
He *bunted* the runner over to second.
She was *bunting* for a base hit, not a sacrifice.

transitivity: both — transitive (bowl a 250 game), intransitive (we bowl on Tuesdays)
gloss: To roll a heavy ball down a lane to knock over pins.
examples: We *bowl* every Tuesday night.
He *bowled* a perfect game in March.
They have been *bowling* in the same league for years.

ru: принимать мяч (в защите), играть в защите
transitivity: both — transitive (field a grounder), intransitive (he fields well)
gloss: To catch or stop a ball that has been hit into play.
examples: Shortstops *field* more balls than anyone else.
He *fielded* the ground ball cleanly and threw to first.
The ball was *fielded* on one hop.

ru: сбивать квотербека с мячом, делать сэк
gloss: In football, to tackle the quarterback before he can throw.
examples: Their front four *sack* the quarterback on almost every third down.
He *sacked* the quarterback three times.
Our passer was *sacked* six times in one half.

ru: идти в блиц, бросать защитников в атаку
transitivity: both — transitive (blitz the quarterback), intransitive (they blitz on every down)
gloss: In football, to rush extra defenders at the quarterback.
examples: They *blitz* on almost every passing down.
The defense *blitzed* and forced a fumble.
He has been *blitzing* off the edge all night.
contrast: Ends in *-tz*, so the third person adds *-es*: *blitzes*.

transitivity: both — transitive (assist the coach), intransitive (assist on a goal)
gloss: To make the pass that lets a teammate score.
examples: Point guards *assist* on most of the scoring.
She *assisted* on both goals in the second half.
He has *assisted* forty times this season.
contrast: In the sports sense you assist **on** a goal or basket, not *assist a goal*.

ru: разворачиваться на опорной ноге, делать пивот
gloss: To turn on one foot while keeping the other foot planted.
examples: Keep one foot down and *pivot*.
He *pivoted* and shot over the defender.
She was *pivoting* toward the basket when she was fouled.
contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so the t does not double: *pivoted*, *pivoting*.

gloss: To bend the flight of a ball with spin, especially on a kick or shot.
examples: He can *curl* a free kick around the wall.
She *curled* the ball into the far corner.
The shot was *curled* just inside the post.

transitivity: both — transitive (aim the ball), intransitive (aim for the corner)
gloss: To point something at a target before hitting or throwing it.
examples: *Aim* for the far corner, not the middle.
She *aimed* at the top of the backboard.
He was *aiming* low and the goalkeeper saved it easily.
contrast: Aim **at** a target you want to hit; aim **for** a result you want to reach.

gloss: To throw something hard and a long way.
examples: Throwers *hurl* the javelin more than eighty meters.
He *hurled* the discus past the record line.
The ball was *hurled* in from deep right field.

ru: подавать эйс, выиграть очко с подачи
gloss: In tennis, to win a point with a serve the opponent cannot touch.
examples: A big server can *ace* you three times in a row.
She *aced* him on match point.
He has *aced* fifteen times in this match alone.

ru: ошибаться на подаче, сделать фол (в теннисе)
gloss: In tennis, to serve the ball into the net or outside the service box.
examples: Nerves make players *fault* on easy serves.
He *faulted* twice and lost the point.
She has *faulted* on three straight first serves.

gloss: To do something so badly that it goes completely wrong.
examples: One slip can *botch* a whole routine.
The goalkeeper *botched* an easy catch.
The handoff was *botched* on the goal line.

gloss: To box or fight in practice, without trying to hurt the other person.
examples: He likes to *spar* three rounds a day.
She *sparred* with two different partners this week.
They have been *sparring* together since Monday.
contrast: The r doubles: *sparred*, *sparring*. You spar **with** a partner.

gloss: To take hold of an opponent and struggle with them at close quarters.
examples: Wrestlers *grapple* for position on the mat.
The two fighters *grappled* against the cage.
They were still *grappling* when the bell rang.
contrast: Grapple **with** an opponent — or, figuratively, **with** a problem.

gloss: To hit someone or something again and again with the fists.
examples: He can *pummel* an opponent for twelve full rounds.
She *pummeled* the heavy bag for an hour.
He was badly *pummeled* in the later rounds.
contrast: American English keeps one l: *pummeled*, *pummeling*. British writing doubles it: *pummelled*.

transitivity: both — transitive (jab him in the ribs), intransitive (jab and move)
gloss: To hit with a short quick straight punch.
examples: *Jab* first, then move to your left.
He *jabbed* his way through the opening round.
She has been *jabbing* at the body all fight.
contrast: One short vowel before a final b, so the b doubles: *jabbed*, *jabbing*.

gloss: To push aside a blow or a shot instead of taking it full on.
examples: Fencers *parry* and then attack in the same motion.
The goalkeeper *parried* the shot over the bar.
He has *parried* everything they have thrown at him.
contrast: Consonant + *-y* becomes *-ies* and *-ied*: *parries*, *parried*, but *parrying* keeps the y.

gloss: To hit someone or something hard enough to move it or bring it down.
examples: One clean right hand can *knock* a fighter down.
He *knocked* his opponent into the ropes.
She was *knocked* off the ball far too easily.
contrast: The k is silent: NAHK, like *knee* and *knife*.

gloss: To throw your body forward suddenly, usually to reach something.
examples: Fencers *lunge* off the back foot.
The goalkeeper *lunged* to his left and just missed it.
He was *lunging* at every ball and missing them all.
contrast: The silent e drops before *-ing*: *lunging*, never *lungeing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (duck a punch), intransitive (duck under the rope)
gloss: To lower your head or body quickly to avoid being hit.
examples: *Duck* under the jab and step inside.
He *ducked* the first punch of the round.
She was *ducking* and weaving for three rounds.

gloss: To bend your knees and lower your body close to the ground.
examples: Sprinters *crouch* behind the blocks before the gun.
The catcher *crouched* low and gave the sign.
He was *crouching* in the ready position the whole point.

gloss: To push or hit someone with your elbow.
examples: Big men *elbow* each other for every rebound.
He *elbowed* a defender and was called for a foul.
She was *elbowed* in the ribs going for the ball.

transitivity: both — transitive (jostle a defender), intransitive (jostle for position)
gloss: To push against other people while trying to get a better position.
examples: Riders *jostle* for position on the first lap.
The two forwards *jostled* in the goalmouth.
He was *jostling* for space near the post.
contrast: The t is silent: JAH-suhl, like *whistle* and *hustle*.

transitivity: both — transitive (hurdle the last barrier), intransitive (she hurdles for the college team)
gloss: To jump over a barrier while running.
examples: Very few athletes can *hurdle* at that speed.
She *hurdled* the last barrier in front and held on.
He has been *hurdling* since his freshman year.

transitivity: both — transitive (vault the bar), intransitive (she vaults last)
gloss: To jump over or across something, often using a pole or your hands.
examples: She will *vault* last in the rotation.
He *vaulted* over the bar at 5.90 meters.
They have been *vaulting* all morning.

gloss: To jump headfirst into water, or to throw yourself through the air for a ball.
examples: Swimmers *dive* from the blocks at the gun.
The goalkeeper *dived* to his right and pushed it wide.
She has *dived* from the ten-meter board twice today.
contrast: Americans say both *dived* and *dove* for the past. *Dived* is the regular form and is always safe; the participle is only *dived*: *has dived*.

gloss: To move over ice or a hard surface on skates.
examples: They *skate* every morning before school.
He *skated* two clean programs in a row.
She has been *skating* since she was four.

gloss: To ride on a skateboard.
examples: Kids *skateboard* in that park all summer.
He *skateboarded* to school every day last year.
She has been *skateboarding* for six years.

ru: ездить на велосипеде, кататься на велосипеде
gloss: To travel or exercise on a bicycle.
examples: We *bike* out to the lake on weekends.
They *biked* twenty miles before lunch.
He has been *biking* to work since March.
contrast: Informal American for *ride a bicycle*. The silent e drops: *biked*, *biking*.

gloss: To ride a bicycle, especially for sport or exercise.
examples: They *cycle* along the river every Sunday.
She *cycled* across the state in five days.
He has been *cycling* competitively for a decade.

gloss: To come down a snowy slope standing on a snowboard.
examples: They *snowboard* every weekend in winter.
He *snowboarded* down the back bowl in the fresh powder.
She has been *snowboarding* since middle school.

gloss: To slide down a snowy hill on a sled.
examples: The kids *sled* on the hill behind the school.
We *sledded* until it got dark.
They have been *sledding* all afternoon.
contrast: One short vowel before a final d, so the d doubles: *sledded*, *sledding*.

gloss: To travel on water in a kayak.
examples: They *kayak* on the bay every summer.
We *kayaked* through the narrow channel.
She has been *kayaking* since college.
contrast: The final k does not double: *kayaked*, *kayaking*, because the stress is on the first syllable.

gloss: To travel on water in a canoe.
examples: We *canoe* down that river every July.
They *canoed* for three days without seeing anyone.
He has been *canoeing* since he was a boy.
contrast: The e stays before *-ing*: *canoeing*, not *canoing*. But it drops before *-ed*: *canoed*.

ru: сплавляться на рафте, сплавляться по реке
transitivity: both — transitive (raft the canyon), intransitive (we rafted all day)
gloss: To travel down a river on a raft.
examples: Tourists *raft* the canyon in June.
We *rafted* the whole gorge in a single day.
They have been *rafting* that river for twenty years.

gloss: To swim just under the surface breathing through a tube.
examples: You can *snorkel* right off the beach here.
We *snorkeled* over the reef for an hour.
They have been *snorkeling* all morning.
contrast: American English keeps one l: *snorkeled*, *snorkeling*. British writing doubles it: *snorkelled*.

gloss: To stay outdoors in a tent for one or more nights.
examples: We *camp* by the lake every August.
They *camped* two nights on the ridge.
He has been *camping* since Friday.

gloss: To walk a long and difficult distance, usually in wild country.
examples: They *trek* through the mountains every spring.
We *trekked* fifteen miles in one day.
She has been *trekking* in Nepal for a month.
contrast: The k doubles: *trekked*, *trekking* — one of the few verbs where a final k is doubled.

gloss: To travel or hike carrying everything you need in a backpack.
examples: Students *backpack* across Europe every summer.
They *backpacked* through the national park.
He has been *backpacking* for a month.

gloss: To play golf.
examples: They *golf* every Saturday morning.
We *golfed* eighteen holes before lunch.
He has been *golfing* since he retired.

gloss: To roll your body forward or backward in a complete circle.
examples: Divers *somersault* twice before entering the water.
He *somersaulted* off the trampoline.
She was *somersaulting* the length of the mat.
contrast: Spelled *-sault*, not *-salt*, and written as one word.

gloss: To make muscles firmer and stronger through exercise.
examples: These exercises *tone* the shoulders and back.
Six weeks of swimming *toned* her legs.
His arms have been *toned* by two years of rowing.

transitivity: both — transitive (hydrate the body), intransitive (hydrate before the race)
gloss: To drink enough water so the body has the fluid it needs.
examples: Runners need to *hydrate* well before a long race.
She *hydrated* between every set.
The players have been *hydrating* all afternoon in this heat.

gloss: To make a physical effort, usually with a reflexive pronoun.
examples: Do not *exert* yourself in this heat.
He *exerted* himself too early in the race.
They were *exerting* themselves far too much in the first half.
contrast: Normally takes a reflexive object: *exert yourself*, *exert himself*, not just *exert*.

gloss: To be extremely good at something.
examples: Few athletes *excel* at two different sports.
She *excelled* in the long jump as a junior.
He has *excelled* at every level of the game.
contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable, so the l doubles: *excelled*, *excelling*. Excel **at** or **in** something.

gloss: To concentrate on one event or skill rather than several.
examples: Some gymnasts *specialize* in a single apparatus.
He *specialized* in the breaststroke from the age of twelve.
She has *specialized* in distance events since high school.
contrast: Specialize **in** something. American spelling uses *-ize*; British writing often prefers *specialise*.

gloss: To tighten painfully, said of a muscle during hard exercise.
examples: Legs often *cramp* in the last mile.
His calf *cramped* at the ninety-minute mark.
She has been *cramping* badly since halftime.

gloss: To shout rude remarks at a player or performer in order to upset them.
examples: Fans *heckle* the visiting kicker on every attempt.
Someone in the front row *heckled* the referee.
He was *heckled* all through his warm-up.

transitivity: both — transitive (the crowd jeered him), intransitive (jeer at a bad call)
gloss: To shout and laugh in a mocking way at someone.
examples: The crowd will *jeer* any bad call.
They *jeered* when he missed the penalty.
The visiting team was *jeered* off the field.
contrast: Intransitively you jeer **at** someone; transitively the object follows directly: *they jeered him*.

gloss: To watch a sporting event instead of taking part in it.
examples: If your knee still hurts, just *spectate* today.
We *spectated* from the top of the hill.
Thousands were *spectating* along the route.

gloss: In chess, to trap the opponent's king so the game is won.
examples: You can *checkmate* him in three moves from here.
She *checkmated* him on move twenty-nine.
He has been *checkmated* twice in a row.

ru: приводить к пату, зайти в тупик
gloss: In chess, to leave the opponent with no legal move, which ends the game in a draw.
examples: One careless move can *stalemate* the game.
He *stalemated* his opponent and saved half a point.
The match was *stalemated* after forty moves.
contrast: A *stalemate* is a draw, not a win — unlike *checkmate*.

transitivity: both — transitive (bluff an opponent), intransitive (he was bluffing)
gloss: To pretend to have a strong hand or position in order to fool an opponent.
examples: Good players *bluff* only when the story makes sense.
She *bluffed* with nothing and won the pot.
He has been *bluffing* all night and nobody noticed.

transitivity: both — transitive (wager fifty dollars), intransitive (wager on the underdog)
gloss: To risk money on the result of a game or race.
examples: Fans *wager* millions on the final every year.
He *wagered* twenty dollars on the underdog.
More has been *wagered* on this game than on any other.
contrast: You wager money **on** a team or a result.

transitivity: both — transitive (cheat your opponent), intransitive (cheat at cards)
gloss: To break the rules secretly in order to win.
examples: Some players *cheat* when nobody is watching.
He *cheated* at cards and was thrown out of the club.
She has never *cheated* in her life.
contrast: You cheat **at** a game, cheat **on** a test, and cheat someone **out of** something.

transitivity: both — transitive (count the points), intransitive (that shot doesn't count)
gloss: To add up points, or to be accepted as valid in the score.
examples: Baskets from behind the line *count* for three points.
The referee *counted* to eight before waving the fight on.
Both free throws were *counted* after the review.

gloss: In card games, to beat a card by playing one of the trump suit.
examples: If you have no hearts, you can *trump* the trick.
She *trumped* my ace and took the hand.
My king was *trumped* on the very last round.

gloss: In a video game, to come back into play after your character is killed.
examples: You *respawn* at the last checkpoint.
He *respawned* right behind the enemy team.
The boss has *respawned* again.

ru: сбивать с ног, отправлять в нокдаун
gloss: To knock someone down to the ground with a punch or a hit.
examples: One good right hand can *floor* him.
She *floored* her opponent in the second round.
He has been *floored* only once in his whole career.

gloss: To fake one way and go the other in order to get past a defender.
examples: Quick running backs *juke* defenders in the open field.
He *juked* the safety and walked into the end zone.
She was *juking* past defenders all game.
contrast: Informal but very common in American sports talk. The silent e drops: *juked*, *juking*.
